title: At Duke Forest in 2013-2015, newer nest boxes had lower ant occupancy and taxon persistence
abstract: We tested whether new nest space had the same ant use as older space in two forest warming arrays. We used HF113 version 61 and compared four old and four newer boxes within each of 15 chambers per site. Complete paired visits gave old and newer ant frequencies of 34.0% and 17.2% at Duke Forest. The paired gap was 16.7 percentage points (95% chamber bootstrap limits 10.3 to 22.9). The Harvard Forest gap was 4.8 points (-0.8 to 10.7). An exploratory exact conditional model matched chamber, census pair and starting taxon. Newer Duke boxes had 0.188 times the odds of retaining the same focal taxon (95% chamber-cluster limits 0.075 to 0.469). The estimate was stable to separate chamber and date removals. A coefficient trained without the test chamber improved conditional retention scores at Duke, but not Harvard. Reoccupation of empty boxes gave uncertain cohort contrasts. The overall warming interaction was not clear in forced-air chambers. The source study already reported warming and persistence effects; our contribution is the cohort comparison, matched transition test and withheld conditional score. These results support a limit after entry at Duke. They do not identify its physical cause or a share of the thermal-tracking gap. Box age, past occupancy, position, colony condition, missing records and only two sites limit inference. The main cohort test preceded the transition analysis; all extensions are marked exploratory. Own code, derived evidence, figures and exact external-data retrieval instructions are included.

display.caption: Old and newer boxes in the same chamber had different use at Duke. The exploratory transition model matches chamber, census interval and starting taxon. Conditional score gains hold out whole chambers. Harvard does not repeat the retention result.
All focal-state cohort slopes in the 12 forced-air chambers per site. Ordinary 95% chamber bootstrap limits are not simultaneous. Multivariate warming interaction tests are uncertain.
